    "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Broad Evidence, and Silently Consistent Precedents"

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I thought I'd serialize my new Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the first Part:.
    • In certain areas, First Amendment precedent turns out to be quite consistent with original meaning—even though the Court hasn't squarely discussed historical evidence in any detail.
    • Recent findings suggest that in some situations, this observation may not be accurate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I thought I'd serialize my new Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the first Part:.

    In certain areas, First Amendment precedent turns out to be quite consistent with original meaning—even though the Court hasn't squarely discussed historical evidence in any detail. This might be a fortunate accident, or perhaps a random coincidence in the policy judgments of the modern Court and the Framing generation. But I expect that some at least stems from a phenomenon that Justice Scalia discussed in McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission (1995): "Principles of liberty fundamental enough to have been embodied within constitutional guarantees are not readily erased from the Nation's consciousness. A governmental practice that has become general throughout the United States, and particularly one that has the validation of long, accepted usage, bears a strong presumption of constitutionality.".

    Recent findings suggest that in some situations, this observation may not be accurate. But in others, there really does appear to be a longstanding constitutional understanding that has become so much part of the law that a court that simply follows doctrine will incorporate original meaning. Let me offer three examples.

    A. "The Liberty of the Press Is Not Confined to Newspapers and Periodicals".

    The Supreme Court has generally held that the First Amendment equally protects all who speak to the public, whether they are professional media (e.g., newspaper publishers or reporters) or nonprofessionals (e.g., leafletters). In this respect, it has treated "the freedom … of the press" as protecting the press as technology—the use of the printing press and its technological heirs—rather than the press as industry, in the sense of people whose daily job is writing for the public.

    In a recent development, now the original articulation of this position in the Supreme Court came in Lovell v. City of Griffin (1938), with little historical analysis:.

    The liberty of the press is not confined to newspapers and periodicals. It necessarily embraces pamphlets and leaflets. These indeed have been historic weapons in the defense of liberty, as the pamphlets of Thomas Paine and others in our own history abundantly attest. The press in its historic connotation comprehends every sort of publication which affords a vehicle of information and opinion.

    It has been revealed that and this is so even though the Court had shown an interest in Framing-era history. Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson (1931) discussed that history in striking down an injunction against the operation of a "scandalous" newspaper. Grosjean v. American Press Co. (1936) discussed history in considerably more detail in holding unconstitutional a selective tax on certain newspapers.

    Sources indicate that more recently, Justice Scalia's concurrence in Citizens United v. FEC (2010) offered a bit more historical analysis:.

    The dissent … interpret[s] the Freedom of the Press Clause to refer to the institutional press (thus demonstrating, according to the dissent, that the Founders "did draw distinctions—explicit distinctions—between types of 'speakers,' or speech outlets or forms"). It is passing strange to interpret the phrase "the freedom of speech, or of the press" to mean, not everyone's right to speak or publish, but rather everyone's right to speak or the institutional press's right to publish. No one thought that is what it meant. Patriot Noah Webster's 1828 dictionary contains, under the word "press," the following entry:.

    "Liberty of the press, in civil policy, is the free right of publishing books, pamphlets or papers without previous restraint; or the unrestrained right which every citizen enjoys of publishing his thoughts and opinions, subject only to punishment for publishing what is pernicious to morals or to the peace of the state.".

    As the Court's opinion describes, our jurisprudence agrees with Noah Webster and contradicts the dissent.

    "The liberty of the press is not confined to newspapers and periodicals. It necessarily embraces pamphlets and leaflets…. The press in its historical connotation comprehends every sort of publication which affords a vehicle of information and opinion.".

    But this is still predominantly a precedential analysis, with one textual argument and one early republican source.

    At the same time, the foundational case in the Court—Lovell—followed 150 years of established practice, to the point that the Court might not have seen the need to do more than just nod to "[t]he press in its historic connotation.".

    As I've laid out elsewhere, Framing-era legal sources, such as cases, treatises, and constitutional provisions, articulated the freedom of the press as extending to everyone, not just to professional newspaper publishers. {See generally Eugene Volokh, Freedom for the Press as an Industry, or for the Press as a Technology? From the Framing to Today, 160 U. Pa. L. Rev. 459 (2012) [hereinafter Volokh, Freedom for the Press]; Eugene Volokh, The Press Clause: Important, Remembered, and Equally Shared, 5 J. Free Speech L. 659 (2025).} Then, starting in the 1820s, courts began to expressly hold that newspaper printers' and editors' rights were equal to everyone else's. In the following decades, that was repeated in case after case throughout the country. By the time Lovell was decided, the principle was well-established in the precedents, and, to my knowledge, unanimously so. The original meaning had made its way into well-settled doctrine and was then ratified by the Court in Lovell.

    The original meaning also fit with practice, which took place in the shadow of the law but which likely also affected the law. In the Framing era, many influential Americans published their views using the printing press, whether in pamphlets or as submissions to newspapers. It would be odd to think that they would have secured special constitutional rights to the just-emerging category of newspapermen, who were in some measure lower status than they were, while denying the same rights to themselves.

    And though those newspapers became relatively more influential in the following centuries, a tradition of leafletting and pamphleteering continued. The Court in 1938 could see the media reality as well as media law and naturally view the nonprofessional leafletter as having the same free press rights as a professional newspaper editor.

    Recent findings suggest that the very first case in which the Supreme Court struck down government action as violating constitutional rights of freedom of expression, Stromberg v. California (1931), involved neither the press nor speech in the literal sense. Rather, it involved what one might today call symbolic expression (or expressive conduct)—the display of a red flag as a revolutionary symbol.

    But the opinion never discussed why displaying a flag counted as "speech" or "press." The opinion below similarly assumed that symbolic expression was as protected as verbal expression, and so did the parties' briefs in the Supreme Court. The Court had neither before nor since analyzed whether this result is consistent with the original meaning of the free expression guarantees. {See Eugene Volokh, Symbolic Expression and the Original Meaning of the First Amendment, 97 Geo. L.J. 1057 (2009).}.

    Likewise, the 1920 California Supreme Court decision in Ex parte Hartman (1920) struck down an earlier law banning the possession or display of flags that represented efforts "espous[ing] for the government of … the United States of America … principles or theories of government antagonistic … to the form of the government thereof as now constituted." The court concluded that Americans have "the right to advocate peaceable changes in our Constitution, laws or form of government," and that therefore "an organization peaceably advocating such changes may adopt a flag … signifying its purpose, and that the display or possession of such flag … cannot be made an unlawful act." The court simply assumed that symbolic expression was constitutionally equivalent to verbal expression, without discussing the matter further.

    It has been revealed that but while these assumptions weren't backed by any originalist analysis, they appear to have been fully consistent with the Framing-era understanding that symbolic expression, pictorial expression, and verbal expression were generally treated as functionally equivalent. This equivalence was most often drawn with regard to restrictions on expression, such as defamation law. But it was also the view taken in the early republic with regard to constitutional protections for expression.

    According to recent reports, thus, for instance, pre-Revolutionary libel law recognized the category of libel by "pictures, signs, and the like"—meaning through symbols, whether printed or physically displayed—as tantamount to libel by writing. Early American law did the same, extending the same principle to incitement to riot as well. Early treatises drew this equivalence. Early court decisions suggested that pictorial and symbolic expression was potentially protected by free expression guarantees (though subject to the same constitutionally permissible restrictions, such as libel law, as verbal expression).

    To offer a particularly vivid illustration, consider the report of Mezzara's Case (1817), apparently the earliest American case involving nonverbal libel—there, a painting of the plaintiff with donkey's ears. The reporter, a Fresh York lawyer, followed the case with a note hypothesizing what would happen if the painting were an apt commentary on the subject's folly and lack of patriotism. In such a situation, the reporter wrote, "[I]f the painter could show the truth of the matter in evidence, as before described, and that he published and exhibited the picture, 'with good motives and for justifiable ends,' … would he not be justifiable under our statute?".

    The statute the reporter cites—which did allow truth as a defense in libel actions, if the defendant acted with good motives and for justifiable ends—was passed in the wake of the Latest York court's evenly dividing in People v. Croswell (1804) on whether the freedom of the press mandated that the defense of truth be allowed in libel prosecutions. The statute implemented Chancellor James Kent's view of the constitutional rule, which was also the view championed by Alexander Hamilton (as Croswell's lawyer) in one of the last public acts of his life, and was seen as an crucial protection for the liberty of the press. And just four years after Mezzara's Case, at the next New York constitutional convention, the statute's provisions were adopted as part of the New York Constitution.

    Industry observers note that the reporter thus saw nothing odd in treating a painting as protected by free expression principles, just as the court saw nothing odd in treating a painting as punishable under libel law principles. Likewise, three-dimensional symbolic expression, such as the raising of a liberty pole, was similarly treated as being potentially constitutionally protected just as pictorial and verbal expression were (though again subject to the possible constitutional limitations imposed on verbal expression).

    Industry observers note that this equivalence of symbolic, pictorial, and verbal expression unsurprisingly endured as part of the law—most often discussed as to libel law—throughout the 1800s and early 1900s. The Supreme Court, for instance, mentioned in 1845 that libel was a "species of defamation which is effected by writing or printing, or by pictures and signs," and in 1904 quoted a law enacted by the Philippine Commission that offered the same definition. There had been hundreds of similar holdings from state courts, whether explicating the common law or state statutes (and often including "effigies" alongside pictures and signs). Legal treatises had set forth the same principle.

    Thus, again, when the cases came before the California Supreme Court in 1920 and the U.S. Supreme Court in 1931, it was natural for the courts and the litigants to casually assume that symbolic expression (there using flags) was likewise treated equivalently to verbal expression for purposes of freedom of expression law. What was accepted in the Framing era continued to be accepted, without any felt need for discussion, in the early 1900s. And here too this conclusion was supported by a long tradition of practice as well as doctrine: Symbolic expression (whether through effigies, processions, visual puns, and the like) was commonplace in the Framing era, and flags and other forms of symbols continued to be used the same way into the 1900s.

    Industry observers note that new York Times Co. v. Sullivan's "actual malice" requirement has of course been criticized as contrary to the original meaning of the First Amendment. But some have also criticized the case on the grounds that it improperly imports freedom of expression principles into civil tort liability. Here too the Court has never tried to explain this particular conclusion on originalist grounds. Likewise, none of the briefs in Sullivan made an originalist argument in favor of applying constitutional limitations to common law civil lawsuits.

    Nonetheless, here too this may have stemmed from the longstanding understanding, dating back to the Framing era, that freedom of expression guarantees did indeed potentially apply to civil liability. We see that starting with 1802 and 1806 decisions from the Vermont and South Carolina high courts, rejecting liability in part by citing the state equivalents of the Petition Clause. {See generally Eugene Volokh, Tort Liability and the Original Meaning of the Freedom of Speech, Press, and Petition, 96 Iowa L. Rev. 249 (2010) (discussing this).}  And we see that in other cases from 1799 onwards that reasoned that constitutional protections may apply to civil lawsuits as well as to criminal prosecutions, but that libelous speech was constitutionally unprotected against civil liability as well as against criminal punishment. Early commentators took the same view.

    Recent findings suggest that and here too the early original meaning turned into well-established constitutional tradition. Throughout the 1800s and 1900s, court decisions routinely assumed that constitutional protections could limit civil liability, though subject to the recognition that there was essentially a First Amendment libel exception for civil as well as criminal liability. By the time of Newly introduced York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964), this position just wasn't particularly controversial, even if the other features of that decision were.

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    "Can AI Ace Your Exam? A Penn Law Experiment," by Prof. R. Polk Wagner

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (449 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I report a controlled experiment that ran a frontier large language model through eleven real University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School final exams in Spring 2026 and sent the machine's answers out for blind grading alongside the work of enrolled students.
    • Industry observers note that first, the model is broadly competitive: across the ten exams returned with grades, it passed every one, sat at or above the class median on every one, and reached the top decile on seven.
    • Second, the benefit of supplying course materials is real but concentrated and uneven.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A very interesting preprint; here's the Abstract:.

    I report a controlled experiment that ran a frontier large language model through eleven real University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School final exams in Spring 2026 and sent the machine's answers out for blind grading alongside the work of enrolled students. Each exam was answered twice: once with no course materials in the model's context (the "no-materials" arm, relying on the model's training alone) and once with the course syllabus and an outline supplied (the "with-materials" arm). Three findings emerge.

    Industry observers note that first, the model is broadly competitive: across the ten exams returned with grades, it passed every one, sat at or above the class median on every one, and reached the top decile on seven. On two exams, both scored on an open, non-saturated scale, it outscored every enrolled student.

    Second, the benefit of supplying course materials is real but concentrated and uneven. It is large on multiple-choice components, small to absent on essays, and on one exam the materials helped the machine's multiple-choice score while hurting its essay—so the gain vanishes when the two are averaged into a single number. The subject of the exam matters as much as its format.

    Third, faculty graders detected the AI submissions at a high rate, but mostly through signals that are easy to remove: formatting artifacts, identification-number placement, even a reversed quotation-mark glyph. The detection that survives those fixes is content-based—two independently generated answers that read as though written by the same hand, and a voice that does not match time-pressured student work. One grader was confident enough in detection to decline to grade the AI answers at all.

    Industry observers note that I read these results less as a verdict than as a measurement problem: when a model that never took the course can top the curve, it is no longer clear that the time-limited, high-stakes final is measuring what we have long assumed it measures—mastery of this course—rather than fluency in a genre the machine commands. That genre was always a contrivance built for grading, not a faithful model of practice, so the machine's success indicates less about lawyering than the headline suggests; but it says a good deal about how much weight the instrument can still bear.

    The urgent ask the experiment surfaces is intentionality: that faculty be clear about what each assessment is meant to measure, and recognize that AI is widening an already-real gap between the law-school exam and the practice it stands in for. The responses will range—from rethinking assessment top to bottom, to narrower adjustments, to simply naming the mismatch and grading with it in view—and reasonable colleagues will differ.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 16, 2026, 12:52 pm CST.

    Recent findings suggest that an Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report. (Image from Shutterstock).

    An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report.

    Anthony Edward Rene Quidera was arrested on Oct. 29 on charges of DUI, exceeding the 65 mph speed limit and possession of an open container.

    Court records show that Quidera was driving his Dodge Charger over 100 mph on the interstate. The arrest report stated that the suspect’s car failed to maintain its lane and was driving on the left median shoulder. After Quidera was stopped, the trooper reported smelling alcohol on his breath.

    Industry observers note that the officer’s probable cause statement ended with the following disclosure: “This report was generated with assistance from Truleo AI. The content reflects the officer’s own observations and recollections. All facts and statements are based solely on the officer’s account,” according to coverage by ABC15 Arizona.

    According to Daniel Fenzel, the commissioner for the Maricopa County Superior Court in Arizona, he was “unable to meaningfully weigh whether the factual allegations made in the narrative (e.g., officer’s observations, signature of affiant officer) were authored, whether in whole or in part, by a generative AI.”.

    Fenzel’s release order stated that the court could not determine probable cause. After being released, Quidera did not show up for his Nov. 12 trial date, according to ABC15 Arizona.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Plaintiff David Egolf was a tenured associate professor at defendant Georgetown University ….

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, from Judge Amy Berman Jackson (D.D.C.) yesterday in Egolf v. Georgetown Univ.:.

    Plaintiff David Egolf was a tenured associate professor at defendant Georgetown University …. In 2015, after an investigation into an internal complaint lodged against Egolf by a Georgetown student, the parties entered into a settlement agreement that placed rules on Egolf's conduct in return for his continued employment at the University. In 2023, following a second report by a recent Georgetown graduate, the University completed another investigation into Egolf and his conduct.

    Industry observers note that egolf filed suit against Georgetown and certain University officials, claiming that the second investigation violated Title IX, Georgetown's Faculty Handbook, and the 2015 settlement agreement. Georgetown has answered the complaint and has filed a counterclaim alleging that Egolf breached the 2015 settlement agreement when he engaged in conduct that violated numerous provisions of the contract. Georgetown seeks compensatory damages and a declaratory judgment….

    In a recent development, according to Georgetown, on September 20, 2013, a student accused Egolf of sexual harassment. Egolf was placed on administrative leave with pay while the University reviewed the student's complaint. The University's Office of Institutional Diversity, Equity, and Affirmative Action ("IDEAA") investigated the claim and, on May 9, 2014, issued a Notice of Findings in which it found, in part, that Egolf:.

    violated the University's Policy Statement on Harassment and Sexual Harassment by making unwelcome sexual advances and engaging in unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature in violation of the policy; engaged in prohibited retaliation against the student; and failed to recognize and ignored the principle underlying [the University's Policy on Consensual Sexual Relationships], which prohibits participation in a professional relationship with a student where there is a conflict of interest.

    Moreover, with respect to the University's alcohol policy and Faculty Handbook, IDEAA found that:.

    (1) [Egolf] served, offered, gave, purchased, and provided alcohol on multiple occasions to [the student] and his roommate, both of whom were underage, and (2) [Egolf] engaged in unfair treatment of [the student], engaged in unprofessional conduct; abused his academic authority over [the student]; engaged in a personal relationship for his own gratification; improperly shared other student information with [the student]; and allowed his objectivity as a professor to be compromised.

    The Notice of Findings recommended that the University consider "the most serious academic and employment sanctions," problem a no-contact directive between Egolf and the student, and require Egolf to remain off campus and have no contact with University students pending the University's decision regarding sanctions. Egolf appealed IDEAA's findings and recommendations, which were later upheld by the University's Equal Opportunity Examining Board on September 14, 2014.

    In a recent development, according to Georgetown, on October 14, 2014, University Provost Robert Groves issued a Termination Letter to Egolf, and then on December 3, 2014, Egolf filed a Notice of Grievance challenging IDEAA's findings and Provost Groves's termination decision. After a closed and confidential conciliation process, on October 15, 2015, the parties entered into an agreement ("2015 Agreement") which permitted Egolf's reinstatement subject to "strict and continuing behavioral restrictions." The 2015 Agreement:.

    The 2015 Agreement also stated that if Egolf had "any questions as to whether a relationship with a student is appropriate," he was required to "immediately disclose the relationship to his chair or dean." ….

    In May 2023, Robert Roe, one of Egolf's former students, started a postbaccalaureate program at Georgetown under Egolf's supervision. While in school, Roe took multiple classes taught by Egolf, served as his Research Assistant over the course of a summer, and was his academic advisee. Georgetown alleges that, on or about July 19, 2023, Roe contacted defendant Samantha Berner, Georgetown's Title IX Coordinator and Director of Title IX Compliance, to raise concerns regarding Egolf's conduct, which Roe characterized as "grooming." ….

    According to Georgetown, on May 6, 2024, IDEAA released a confidential investigative report stating that there was "sufficient evidence under a preponderance of the evidence standard to substantiate a finding" of Egolf's sexual misconduct, resulting in violations of University policy, the Faculty Handbook, and the 2015 Agreement…. The IDEAA investigative report found that Egolf maintained a "personal and social relationship with a student that he advised, including frequent non-academic communications, social outings, private meetings, and sustained personal involvement extending beyond appropriate faculty-student boundaries." Egolf admitted the truth of certain factual findings in his appeal by stating, "[t]his statement is true," including:.

    In a recent development, according to Georgetown, in Egolf's appeal, he further admitted that he and Roe had meals together "about once a month" at a restaurant near the University where they would discuss academic and personal topics. The meals initially included other students and alumni but later became more often one-on-one. Egolf also allegedly admitted that:.

    [Egolf] invited Mr. [Roe] to spend the night at his house after their celebration of Mr. [Roe]'s graduation, since they expected to drink and it would be late. [Egolf] invited Mr. [Roe] to spend the night at his house after they went to see the Lion King so that he would not have to drive to Mr. [Roe]'s home in Reston and back the night immediately preceding when Mr. [Roe] was already slated to go to [Egolf]'s home for their graduation celebration.

    According to Georgetown, Egolf stated in his appeal that he and the student consumed three-and-a-half bottles of champagne together that same evening; he left the door slightly ajar when he went into the bathroom; he told Roe stories about being propositioned by a student and finding a student naked on his couch; he made a joke about his college friend's genitalia; and he participated in conduct related to a drinking game.

    Georgetown also alleges that Egolf provided Roe with private study sessions, inflated his grades in a manner inconsistent with academic evaluation standards, and substantially assisted in drafting a portion of his undergraduate thesis and grant application.

    Moreover, Egolf allegedly texted Roe that, upon Roe's graduation, Egolf would be able to tell him "all of the crazy stories I've hinted at" and did share the explicit stories following graduation; engaged in discussions about nudity and other sexual topics; made a joke involving genitalia; and teased Roe while offering to help remove his pants. Finally, Georgetown alleges that Egolf failed to disclose the nature or extent of his relationship with Roe to any University administrator as required by the 2015 Agreement…..

    Egolf was eventually fired. Before the firing (but after he was put on paid leave), he sued, alleging Title IX retaliation, breach of contract, and other matters, and Georgetown counterclaimed, "alleging breach of the 2015 Agreement and breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing," and seeking compensatory damages for the costs of various proceedings (including the legal costs of defending the lawsuit). The court allowed the claims to go forward; an excerpt:.

    To state a claim for breach of contract, "it is enough for the plaintiff to describe the terms of the alleged contract and the nature of the defendant's breach." Contrary to Egolf's assertions, a plaintiff need not allege damages caused by the breach to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss…. Georgetown claims that Egolf violated the agreement by:.

    Finally, Georgetown identifies the five specific provisions of the 2015 Agreement they allege that Egolf violated.

    Even if Egolf is correct that Georgetown must allege damages to state a claim, the Court does not find that, on the face of the counterclaim, consequential damages were outside the contemplation of the parties at the time of the contract…. [P]aragraph 11 of the Agreement demonstrates that the parties expressly contemplated the possibility of litigation. Ex. A at 11 ("Any breach, or actions taken upon breach, of the Agreement by either party may also be enforced by filing suit, or seeking an injunction, in a court of competent jurisdiction"). Resolving all reasonable inferences in Georgetown's favor, the Court does not find that legal damages were beyond the contemplation of the 2015 Agreement.

    Brian Drockton and Henry Adam Platt (Saul Ewing LLP) represent Georgetown.

The results are worth a careful study to forecast the future religious landscape in the United States, and how those numbers will affect debates about religious liberty. Here is a summary:.

    The United States is expected to follow roughly the same pattern of religious change as the overall North American region.5 By 2070, Christians are expected to decline to less than half of the U.S. population, while religiously unaffiliated people will rise to about 41%. And Jews – who were the country's third-largest religious group in 2020 – will be outnumbered by both Muslims and Hindus in 2070 if recent demographic trends continue.

    Recent findings suggest that if recent demographic trends continue, Israel will be home to 62% of the global Jewish population in 2070, up from 46% in 2020. During this 50-year time span, the number of Jews living in Israel is forecast to grow from 6.8 million to 11.1 million, due primarily to what demographers call "natural increase": the number of births exceeding the number of deaths in a population.

    Sources indicate that I've written on this blog before that I can see a future where my family and I will have to move to Israel. The events of the last election make that outcome seem just-that-much-more likely. And remember, the persecution of Jews will always be a precursor to persecution of other faiths.

    Ultimately, debates about religious liberty will look very different as the composition of religious group changes. I would note that at the recent Federalist Society convention, there was a brief mention about the risks of Shariah Law--a topic that I can't ever recall being discussed on a FedSoc platform. USDA Secretary's Memorandum 1078-019.     Industry observers note that on July 4, 2025, Secretary [of Agriculture Brooke] Rollins sent an email from her official email account celebrating Independence Day. The message was sent to all USDA employees. Her message concluded with a written statement, "May God continue to protect the United States of America and may His favor shine over all her land." On November 26, 2025, Rollins sent a Thanksgiving message from her official email account to all USDA employees, attributing the first Thanksgiving in part to "gratitude towards a loving God.".

On December 23, 2025, Rollins emailed USDA employees a Christmas message containing a video in which she stated that "The spirit of generosity flows from the very first Christmas when God gave us the greatest gift possible, the gift of his Son and our Savior Jesus Christ, who came to free us from our sins and open the door to eternal life. This is the reason for the season….".

    On April 5, 2026, she sent an Easter email addressed to "All USDA Employees" which read:.

    Happy Easter – He is Risen indeed!

    Today we celebrate the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind.

    From the foot of the Cross on Good Friday to the stone rolled away from the now empty tomb, sin has been destroyed. Jesus has been raised from the dead. And God has granted each of us victory and fresh life. And where there is life — risen life — there is hope.

    No matter the very real trials and hardships we face, fear and sin and death do not get the last word. Because on Easter morning, "Hell took a body, and discovered God. It took earth, and encountered Heaven. It took what it saw, and was overcome by what it did not see." Now that is reason to rejoice!

    And so, like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for.

    Please know how amazed and grateful I am for the hard work each of you do to support our shared mission here at USDA. I hope you and your loved ones have a truly blessed and happy Easter. May God continue to bless you, your families, and our exceptional country, One Nation, Under God.

    At the top of the email, Secretary Rollins included an illustration of a stone rolled away from Jesus' tomb with the words "Christ is Risen" written above the illustration.

    According to recent reports, plaintiffs allege that Rollins has not sent comparable messages acknowledging other religions' holidays. They contrast her communications with USDA's November 20, 2025 guidance on religious expression, which provides that officials "[c]annot use official authority to pressure subordinates" regarding religious beliefs and "[m]ust stop if a colleague asks [them] to stop." They further allege that Rollins defended the Easter message publicly and is likely to send similar communications marking future Christian holidays.

    Each individual plaintiff received and read the challenged messages. Plaintiffs allege that they are expected to read communications from the Secretary because those communications may contain consequential workplace information. Other messages have addressed agency reorganization, employee relocation, changes to USDA's civil rights program, shutdown planning, and the Deferred Resignation Program; holiday messages have historically included administrative-leave announcements.

    Industry observers note that the individual plaintiffs allege that the messages convey a preference for employees who share the Secretary's Christian beliefs, make them feel excluded, and pressure them to conceal their own beliefs or appear to share hers. They fear workplace disfavor and retaliation for objecting; the complaint also alleges that supervisors have warned that objections would result in "trouble." Plaintiff Poopatanapong alleges that she no longer feels safe discussing a Buddhist holiday she celebrates; Roberts, an atheist, feels silenced; and Wolfe, a Pagan, feels pressure to appear Christian to advance professionally. alleges that its USDA members likewise received the messages, felt compelled to read them, and experienced pressure to accept the Secretary's beliefs while withholding their own.

    The court held that plaintiffs' Establishment Clause were likely violated:.

    The Establishment Clause protects religious freedom by "command[ing] a separation of church and state." Kennedy v. Bremerton Sch. Dist., 597 U.S. 507, 558–59 (2022) (citing Cutter v. Wilkinson, 544 U.S. 709, 719 (2005)). [Note that this quote is actually from Justice Sotomayor's dissent in Kennedy, though it appears in the Cutter majority. -EV] At its core, this means forbidding "sponsorship, financial support, and active involvement of the sovereign in religious activity." As the Supreme Court acknowledged in Kennedy, the Establishment Clause does not "'compel the government to purge from the public sphere' anything an objective observer could reasonably infer endorses or 'partakes of the religious.'" However, courts must be cautious to ensure that "what might begin as a tolerant expression of religious views" does not "end in a policy to indoctrinate and coerce.".

    According to recent reports, to determine whether government action violates the Establishment Clause, the Court must "focus[ ] on original meaning and history" of the First Amendment. That is, this Court's must be guided by "historical practices and understandings" of the relationship between government and religion in America. Pursuant to this approach, any practice that was "accepted by the Framers and has withstood the critical scrutiny of time and political change" does not violate the Establishment Clause. The analysis does not end merely because a practice has been observed in the past. The history and tradition test requires this Court to look to the "uninterrupted practice" of law in our nation's traditions.

    Traditionally, the hallmark of government conduct violative of the Establishment Clause is the presence of some form of coercion upon its citizens.

    Sources indicate that thomas Jefferson and James Madison, the two Founders most instrumental in the drafting and ratification of the Religion Clauses of the First Amendment, articulated a founding-era concern broader than direct, compelled sectarian practices. Madison, for example, expressed concern that even instances of governmental "recommendation[]" concerning religion "naturally terminate[] in a conformity to the creed of the majority []." Jefferson expressed concern about indirect forms of coercion such as conduct which might invite "some degree of proscription perhaps in public opinion." Most fitting, in his "Memorial and Remonstrance Against Religious Assessments" drafted in 1785, Madison questioned the ends sought by the promotion of a sectarian underpinning to our country's political foundation: "Who does not see that the same authority which can establish Christianity, in exclusion of all other Religions, may establish with the same ease any particular sect of Christians, in exclusion of all other Sects?" His guidance, contained in the same writings: "Such a Government will be best supported by protecting every Citizen in the enjoyment of his Religion with the same equal hand which protects his person and his property; by neither invading the equal rights of any Sect, nor suffering any Sect to invade those of another." The Founders may have lacked the foresight to account for contemporary technological advances, but the principles embedded in our First Amendment ring as true today. As difficult as the task may be, below, this Court faithfully applies the founding-era's understanding of the Establishment Clause to the modern-day circumstances giving rise to this litigation….

    After reviewing and weighing the Establishment Clause jurisprudence, the Court finds that Secretary Rollins appears to exploit her position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion. Here, three factors inform the Court's conclusion that the Secretary's conduct was coercive: (1) her position of authority, (2) the use of her official email to send messages to all USDA employees, and (3) the alienating language contained in the emails to employees who did not share her religious tenets. [Detailed discussion of factors 1 and 2 omitted for space reasons. -EV].

    It makes no difference that the emails did not single out dissidents, disparage those who did not share the Secretary's beliefs, or indicate work-related decisions would be influenced by an employees' reaction to the emails. The Supreme Court has repeatedly recognized that "immense social pressure" can result in a finding of coercion. Such pressure is demonstrated here…. While social pressure alone is not state coercion because "mature adults … presumably are not readily susceptible to religious indoctrination or peer pressure[,]" the totality of the circumstances here demonstrates such immense pressure to amount to coercion….

    The Court does not purport to regulate the religiosity of the Secretary—nor could it. "A relentless and all-pervasive attempt to exclude religion from every aspect of public life could itself become inconsistent with the Constitution." Nor does this Court generally condemn the expression of religious sentiments. Instead, this Court requires the Secretary to observe her own directives. USDA Secretary's Memorandum 1078-019. The April 5, 2026, and December 23, 2025, messages go too far. They suggest acquiescence that amounts to coercive pressure; a pressure of conformity sufficient to raise an Establishment Clause violation….

    Retrospective Voting and the 2026 Election

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In my book Democracy and Political Ignorance  and various other writings going all the way back to my very first academic article (published in 1998), I have warned of the dangers of widespread voter ignorance.
    • Sources indicate that retrospective voting is probably the most often-used information shortcut, and the one most cited by scholars who argue that voter ignorance isn't much of a problem.
    • If things are going well, you vote to reelect them to continue their good work.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In my book Democracy and Political Ignorance  and various other writings going all the way back to my very first academic article (published in 1998), I have warned of the dangers of widespread voter ignorance. And I have argued that "information shortcuts" - small bits of knowledge that supposedly make up for ignorance about details - are generally ineffective or even counterproductive. Thus, I should acknowledge that one of those shortcuts - retrospective voting - worked fairly well in the recently concluded 2026 election. At the same time, the problem of political ignorance remains a grave menace.

    Sources indicate that retrospective voting is probably the most often-used information shortcut, and the one most cited by scholars who argue that voter ignorance isn't much of a problem. The basic idea is simple: to be a good voter you don't need to know much about government and public policy. You just need to know whether things are going well or badly under the rule of the incumbents.

    If things are going well, you vote to reelect them to continue their good work. If badly, you vote to "throw the bastards out." Then you elect a newly introduced set of bastards in their place; but the new bastards will hopefully know they need to do a good job, else they will get thrown out in their turn, at the next election. As Ronald Reagan famously put it during the 1980 election, "Next Tuesday all of you will go to the polls… I think when you make that decision it might be well if you would ask yourself: Are you better off than you were four years ago?".

    I and other critics have long pointed out that, when ignorant voters use the retrospective voting shortcut, they often end up rewarding and punishing incumbents for things they did not cause (usually short-term economic trends), while ignoring more subtle long-term problems. In addition, they often don't know which officials are responsible for which issues, and tend to overlook the possibility that the opposition party's policies will be as bad or worse.

    Sources indicate that nonetheless, retrospective voting actually worked pretty well in the 2026 election. As I noted in a previous post, polls show that many voters punished the Republicans for high prices caused by Trump's tariffs,  the failed Iran War, and the administration's cruel campaign of mass deportations (which particularly angered Hispanic voters in key states and congressional districts). One can also add the issue of corruption, which polls  indicate also had a significant impact.

    Sources indicate that the Republicans really were responsible for all three of these policies. They weren't caused by exogenous factors outside of Trump's control. And the policies really did have massive negative effects in raising prices, an unsuccessful war, and massive cruelty and violations of civil liberties caused by the deportation campaign. The scope and effects of corruption are harder to measure. But this administration may be the most corrupt in American history. And, on all four issues, the Democrats are likely to be at least somewhat better.

    But while retrospective voting worked reasonably well in the 2026 midterm election, we cannot conclude that the problem of political ignorance doesn't matter, or even that it's overblown. Rather, the shortcut was effective primarily because of the large and obvious nature of Trump's failures.

    Sources indicate that along with other scholars, I have long recognized that retrospective voting can be effective if incumbents screw in ways that have large and obvious bad effects - ones that even very ignorant voters can easily see and understand. For example, I often cite economist Amartya Sen's famous finding that mass famines never or almost never occur under democracies (even as they happen much more often under dictatorships). Even ignorant voters will notice a famine is going on, blame incumbents for it, and vote accordingly.

    Trump's failures over the last two years weren't quite as bad as a mass famine. But they were nonetheless large (including a major war and  the highest tariff schedule since the Great Depression), highly visible, and many of their effects were easy to understand. It isn't hard to notice that massive tariff increases cause prices to rise. The war and its effects on prices were also highly visible. Images of brutal deportations and resulting civil liberties violations were all over the news. Most voters probably didn't know about the details of the administration's corruption. But there was so much of it, that most probably heard at least something about it.

    Many policy failures are far less readily apparent than that. And ignorant voters are therefore likely to overlook or misunderstand them. It's not hard to find examples even in the 2026 election itself. To take a particularly key case, the US faces a massive looming fiscal crisis, caused in large part by the combination of an aging population and out-of-control entitlement spending. Yet most candidates of both parties largely ignored this problem, and promise continued massive spending, and avoiding tax increases for almost everyone, except perhaps a few billionaires and other very wealthy people. They could do that because surveys show most voters are ignorant about our fiscal situation and especially don't realize the key role of entitlement spending.

    Voters' justified negative reaction in 2026 to tariffs, mass deportations, corruption, and the Iran War also highlight the failure of information shortcuts in the 2024 election. At that time, it was evident to informed observers that Trump would seek to institute massive tariffs and cruel deportation policies. Indeed, I myself was among those who cited them as among the principal reasons to oppose Trump in that election. Large-scale corruption was also predictable, given Trump's long history of skullduggery. Yet swing voters got these complications wrong - despite the fact that high prices were a major issue in 2024, and tariffs and mass deportations would predictably raise them (as I also pointed out at the time).

    The Iran War was admittedly less predictable. Trump even promised to avoid fresh wars. But his well-documented combination of ignorance and impulsiveness meant that returning him to office created a significant risk of a foreign policy crisis spiraling out of control.

    According to recent reports, and on all these concerns, it was predictable (and predicted by many, including me) that Trump 2.0 would surround himself with cronies and loyalists likely to indulge his worst instincts. No longer would he be constrained by "adults in the room," as occasionally happened during his first term.

    Thus, while an information shortcut worked well in 2026, it's key to recognize that was only necessary because shortcuts failed miserably in 2024, which was an only modestly more difficult situation. In that earlier election, we did not yet see the effects of Trump's awful second-term policies. But most of those policies and effects were readily predictable by any moderately well-informed observer. Yet most swing voters were much more ignorant than that, and thus instead voted to punish Democrats for high prices, ignoring the high likelihood that electing Trump would make that problem worse, not better.

    In addition, as I emphasized in my November 2024 post on voter ignorance in that year's election, a combination of ignorance and bias led many voters to underestimate the significance of Trump's assault on basic norms and principles of liberal democracy.

    It is also key to remember that the problem of voter ignorance is not just that it leads voters to make "wrong" choices between the options put before them. It also makes those options worse in the first place. As I have long argued in my book and elsewhere, political ignorance also makes those options worse in the first place. Politicians and campaign strategists know they face a largely ignorant electorate, and act accordingly. Sweeping the fiscal crisis under the rug is just one of many examples of that tendency. Even if information shortcuts consistently helped voters choose the lesser of the evils before them (which, sadly, they don't!), ignorance would still make those options much more evil than they would be otherwise.

    According to recent reports, trump is a particularly egregious long-time exploiter of political ignorance, which played key roles in his rise and return to power. But more conventional politicians also routinely exploit it, as Barack Obama did, for example. For those keeping score, I have been arguing that political ignorance is a serious danger for over 25 years, under both Republican and Democratic administrations, and through many changes in the political winds.

    The  2024 election led me to conclude that voter ignorance was an even more serious problem than I previously thought. This year's election is, perhaps, a data point for the other side. But whether or not the problem is worse than I thought before 2024, it continues to be a serious danger.

    Industry observers note that there is no easy fix for widespread voter ignorance. I assessed  various possible options in my 2023 book chapter on "Top-Down and Bottom-Up Solutions to the Problem of Political Ignorance, and in Chapters 5-7 of Democracy and Political Ignorance. I think the most promising approach make fewer decisions at the ballot box and more by "voting with your feet," where incentives to seek out information and use it wisely are better. I also argue in both works that the idea of simply paying voters to increase their knowledge deserves more attention. But any remedy will take time, and we may need a combination of several strategies, not just one.

    Sources indicate that in sum, the 2026 election is an example of retrospective voting working relatively well. But we should not conclude this shortcut - or any other - is a good general solution to the problem of widespread political ignorance.

    A former Cravath, Swaine & Moore employee who was arrested on charges of insider trading last week is reportedly considering a plea deal.

    Federal prosecutors in Fresh York allege that Chetram Balli, who is also known as Tony Balli, 54, accessed nonpublic information through his role as a document processing specialist for Cravath and traded ahead of at least five of the law firm’s major deals.

    According to Law360, a one-page form order signed Thursday by U.S. Magistrate Judge Marcia M. Henry of the Eastern District of New York reveals that federal prosecutors and Balli are engaged in plea discussions.

    The order also demonstrates that Balli’s defense counsel requested more time to focus on negotiations without the risk of not being adequately prepared for a trial, Law360 reports.

    Law360 requested but did not receive comment from either party.

    In a recent development, balli began working for Cravath in 1989. According to prosecutors, he supported attorneys by producing legal documents and U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filings and at times had access to confidential information.

    Balli was arrested Thursday after prosecutors filed a criminal complaint against him and alleged that he made more than $70,000 in illicit profits.

    Trump Justice Department Drops Attempt to Block Certification of Alaska Senate Election Result in "Voter Confusion" Case

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (453 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, I previously wrote about the Trump Justice Department's lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Alaska Senate election results, and the district court ruling rejecting it.
    • Today, as reported by prominent election law scholar Rick Hasen, DOJ filed a brief in the US Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit seeking to dismiss the case.
    • This brings to an end a lawsuit that was always a turkey of a case (though perhaps calling it that is an insult to turkeys!).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, I previously wrote about the Trump Justice Department's lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Alaska Senate election results, and the district court ruling rejecting it. The Trump DOJ argued that blocking the  results was necessary to prevent "voter confusion" caused by the presence of two candidates with very similar names on the ballot. As I  explained previously, Republican candidate Dan J. Sullivan can potentially be confused with Dan S. Sullivan (the incumbent GOP senator), and some voters might have accidentally chosen Dan J. even though they intended to back Dan S.

    Today, as reported by prominent election law scholar Rick Hasen, DOJ filed a brief in the US Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit seeking to dismiss the case. They also want the district court ruling vacated for procedural reasons (I will not opine on whether that's warranted).

    This brings to an end a lawsuit that was always a turkey of a case (though perhaps calling it that is an insult to turkeys!). As explained in my post on the district court ruling and in an excellent amicus brief filed by Rick Hasen, the case never had any merit, and a court decision ruling in its favor would have set a dangerous precedent.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition, the election results show that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola got an absolute majority of the vote (about 50.1%), more than both Dan Sullivans and all other candidates combined. Thus, even if all of the 1.7% of voters who chose Dan J. actually intended to back Dan S., it made no difference. Alaska's system of ranked choice voting (under which, if no candidate gets a majority in the first round, votes get reallocated) might have further reduced any problem. But no reallocation took place here, because Peltola got an absolute majority to begin with. This is likely what led DOJ to finally thrown in the towel.

    As noted in one of my earlier posts about the case, Democrats may well deserve blame for seeking to deceive voters in this way, even though it was never likely to change the result (evidence indicates Dan J. may have gotten on the ballot as part of a Democratic effort to siphon off voters from Dan S.). But for reasons outlined in the same post, this kind of thing is far from the worst example of exploitation of voter ignorance.

    Peltola's win was mostly just part of the broader "Blue tsunami" which saw the Democratis gain 9 Senate seats, including in several traditional red states. But perhaps Peltola got over the top because of the immense popularity of her pet lizard! We could use more lizards on Capitol Hill.

    Recent findings suggest that district attorneys and victims’ families have taken their fight to the California Supreme Court over California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s initiative to commute over 500 death row penalty sentences.

    The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, which represents the plaintiffs, argued Monday that the governor was required to give formal notice to district attorneys before commuting 548 death penalty sentences. The plaintiffs also challenged Newsom’s broad death penalty commutations without considering individual circumstances, beyond whether a person has more than one felony conviction. Existing law permits crime victims the opportunity to speak before a governor can commute someone.

    “Gov. Newsom decided his personal views should override all those who actually participated in the process, followed and applied the law,” the plaintiffs mentioned. “He did none of that, as he freely admits. That alone is an abuse of power that must not stand,” according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

    It has been revealed that newsom declared Nov. 5 the commutations of all people on death row to life in prison without parole. The governor wrote a letter that said state-sanctioned killing undermines the legal system’s foundation and counters California’s values.

    Newsom, who has served two terms, declared a moratorium on all executions in 2019 and leaves office in January.

    Newsom moves to commute 548 death sentences, emptying California’s death row.

    Tech Report: Second Amendment Roundup: Major New Film "Firearms and the AR-15 Rifle"

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that "Firearms and the AR-15 Rifle: A Primer for the Bench and Bar" is the title of a latest and important film designed to help judges and legal professionals understand the mechanics and features of modern firearms, including the AR-15 semiautomatic rifle.
    • This is a critical time to inform the bench and the bar about the operation of the AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles, given the ongoing legal fights over modern semiautomatic firearms including the pending Supreme Court cases of Viramontes v.
    • Industry observers note that the film was written, directed and produced by law professor and Second Amendment scholar Mark W.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that "Firearms and the AR-15 Rifle: A Primer for the Bench and Bar" is the title of a latest and important film designed to help judges and legal professionals understand the mechanics and features of modern firearms, including the AR-15 semiautomatic rifle. The film is available on YouTube and on Rumble. Following my brief introduction, firearms expert Richard Vasquez takes the center stage. After 21 years in the Marine Corps as an advanced gunsmith and ordnance officer, Mr. Vasquez served for 14 years in the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), including time within the Firearms Technology Branch. He is now a firearms consultant.

    This is a critical time to inform the bench and the bar about the operation of the AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles, given the ongoing legal fights over modern semiautomatic firearms including the pending Supreme Court cases of Viramontes v. Cook County and Grant v. Higgins. This film sticks to the facts about the operations and mechanics of modern firearms without touching upon any of the legal or political debates about the AR-15. It does a particularly good job explaining the various features found on most AR-15 rifles and does a great job explaining the differences between semiautomatic firearms and other types of modern firearms, including fully-automatic machine guns.

    Industry observers note that the film was written, directed and produced by law professor and Second Amendment scholar Mark W. Smith, who was most recently seen discussing firearms and the American Revolution on the Federalist Society annual convention panel "When in the Course of Human Events" (at 22:30).

    Sources indicate that the film begins with a historical overview of the development of firearms, from single-shot flintlocks to today's semiautomatics. The film describes the basic components of firearms and rifles, in particular. It explains what makes gas-operated semiautomatic rifles different from lever action, bolt action and pump action rifles. The film then goes on to show in great detail how a gas-operated semiautomatic rifle operates.

    Industry observers note that spoiler alert:  I suspect that one of the film's biggest contributions to the public discourse on semiautomatic firearms will be its easy-to-understand graphics and animations. Thanks to many colorful images, video clips, animations as well as Vasquez's break downs of modern firearm mechanics and operations, I suspect this film will become a valuable teaching tool for people interested in firearms including judges and legal professionals.

    According to recent reports, getting to the technical aspects, Mr. Vasquez explains the AR-15 firing mechanism, beginning with the insertion of a cartridge into the chamber, pulling of the trigger, activation of the sear, release of the bolt and firing pin, striking of the primer, explosion of the powder, discharge of the bullet, bleeding of gas causing the bolt carrier group to retract, elimination of the spent cartridge, and insertion of a new cartridge from the magazine to the chamber, thus beginning a new firing cycle. Easy to follow diagrams of each process in that order simplify and bring to life what happens each step of the way.

    In a recent development, next, Mr. Vasquez moves onto the outward features typical of the AR-15 platform. The telescoping stock allows the shoulder stock to be adjusted for different statures, such as two spouses, or seasonal clothing, like an overcoat while hunting. The pistol grip and straight-line stock reduce recoil and muzzle jump, allowing a second, more accurate shot. The handguard (barrel shroud) with Picatinny Rail facilitates various attachments like iron sights, scopes, and flashlights. A threaded barrel can be equipped with a flash suppressor to reduce blindness when firing at night or with a muzzle brake to lesson recoil.

    Two aspects of the operational process are worth emphasis. First, nothing about the AR-15 rifle itself dictates the number of rounds it will fire before needing to reinsert a fresh magazine. That depends on the magazine, which may hold 5, 10, 20, or 30 rounds. Second, while firing a shot automatically loads a new cartridge into the chamber, firing the next shot requires that the trigger be pulled again. That distinguishes a semiautomatic from a fully automatic, aka a machine gun, which requires only the trigger to be depressed and held down to fire all rounds in the magazine.

    It's my belief that "Firearms and the AR-15 Rifle: A Primer for the Bench and Bar" will become the definitive documentary on the mechanics of the AR-15 and modern semiautomatic rifles.

    Fourth Circuit Panel Splits Three Ways on Kalshi Preemption

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Yesterday, in KalshiEX LLC v Martin, a three-judge panel of the U.S.
    • In the end, two judges (Gregory and Thacker) concluded state regulation of these contracts is not preempted, but split over whether the contracts at concern are "swaps." (Judge Thacker concluded they are not, but Judge Gregory concluded there is no need to resolve that question.) A third judge (Benjamin) concluded that Kalshi's sporting event contracts are swaps and are preempted.
    • KalshiEX, LLC ("Kalshi") brings this appeal, which presents a narrow question of federal preemption.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Yesterday, in KalshiEX LLC v Martin, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit split three ways on whether sporting event contracts offered by Kalshi are "swaps" (as opposed to sports gambling), and whether state regulation of such contracts is preempted by federal law. The court's ultimate opinion was a one sentence per curiam affirming the district court, with two concurrences and a dissent.

    In the end, two judges (Gregory and Thacker) concluded state regulation of these contracts is not preempted, but split over whether the contracts at concern are "swaps." (Judge Thacker concluded they are not, but Judge Gregory concluded there is no need to resolve that question.) A third judge (Benjamin) concluded that Kalshi's sporting event contracts are swaps and are preempted. So that's two votes against preemption, and two votes that whether Kalshi's contracts are swaps should determine whether they are preempted.

    Judge Gregory began his concurrence as follows:.

    KalshiEX, LLC ("Kalshi") brings this appeal, which presents a narrow question of federal preemption. The Commodity Exchange Act ("CEA" or "the Act") grants the Commodity Futures Trading Commission ("CFTC") exclusive jurisdiction over transactions involving swaps traded or executed on a designated contract market ("DCM"). 7 U.S.C. § 2(a)(1)(A). But Congress also enacted a separate provision elsewhere in the same Act providing separate treatment for certain event contracts specifically involving gaming, among other things, and providing that certain such contracts may not be listed or traded on a DCM. Id. § 7a-2(c)(5)(C)(i)–(iii). The question here is whether, when read together, those provisions clearly establish that the CFTC's authority over the sports event contracts at matter excludes Maryland's traditionally recognized authority to enforce its gaming laws.

    I do not decide whether Kalshi's sports event contracts are "swaps" within the meaning of the CEA. That is because, even assuming they are, neither the Act nor the CFTC's implementation of it clearly establish that such contracts are entitled to trade on a DCM free from state gaming laws. Whether the contracts are swaps bears on the scope of the CFTC's regulatory authority; it does not alone answer whether that authority is exclusive to the CFTC and displaces Maryland's concurrent authority to regulate gambling. Rather than providing a settled answer, the statutory and regulatory framework leaves unresolved the relationship between the CEA's grant of exclusive jurisdiction and Congress's treatment of gaming contracts.

    Because the regulation of gambling has long been a matter of traditional state police power, I would not infer that Congress displaced Maryland's concurrent authority absent a clear expression of its intent to do so. Nor has Kalshi shown that complying with both the CEA and the Maryland law at problem would be impossible or stand as an obstacle to Congress's objective to create a centralized federal regulatory framework for trading derivative contracts. I therefore conclude that Kalshi has not demonstrated that the CEA preempts Maryland's sports wagering laws and concur in the judgment affirming the district court.

    Recent findings suggest that judge Thacker concurred separately, as she saw the complications differently, only she reached the same bottom-line result. Her opinion begins:.

    Although I ultimately concur in the bottom line opinion, that is, affirmance of the district court, I get there via a different route than does my concurring colleague. KalshiEX, LLC ("Appellant") operates a prediction market. On that market, people enter into contracts with one another in which they try to predict whether or not a given event will occur. This appeal focuses on Appellant's sporting event based contracts. For instance, a user can predict whether a given NASCAR driver will win Talladega, or whether a college basketball team will win or lose a particular game. If the prediction is correct, the user gets paid. If not, they lose money.

    It has been revealed that in this appeal, we are asked whether Appellant's sporting event based contracts are "swaps" as defined by the Commodity Exchange Act ("CEA"). In my view, Appellant's sporting event based contracts are not swaps within the meaning of the CEA. See also, KalshiEX, LLC v. Assad, No. 25-7516, 2026 WL 2543846 (9th Cir. Aug. 28, 2026). As a result, I would hold that Appellant's contracts lie beyond the exclusive regulatory authority of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission ("CFTC"). Therefore, Maryland officials can co-regulate these contracts.

    And Judge Benjamin, dissenting, began her opinion this way.

    It has been revealed that this case concerns whether the Commodity Exchange Act ("CEA") preempts Maryland's application of its gambling laws to KalshiEX's ("Kalshi") sports related event contracts traded on a federally regulated exchange. Kalshi argues that because it operates as a designated contract market ("DCM") under the CEA, its contracts fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission ("CFTC"). Maryland argues that Kalshi's contracts are functionally indistinguishable from sports betting and thus remain subject to traditional state authority over gambling.

    This appeal turns on two issues: (1) whether Kalshi's sporting event contracts are "swaps" under the CEA and, if so, (2) whether the CEA preempts otherwise applicable state law. Because I think Kalshi's sports-related event contracts are "swaps" under the CEA, and because Congress has granted "exclusive jurisdiction" over such swaps to the CFTC, I would vacate the district court's denial of the preliminary injunction and remand for further proceedings. I respectfully dissent.

    Sources indicate that this question is certainly headed to the Supreme Court, whether in this case or one of the others. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, in a split decision, found preemption was likely (in reviewing a preliminary injunction), whereas the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the Ninth and Sixth Circuits found Kalshi's arguments for preemption unpersuasive. I am personally skeptical of preemption here, but we will see whether that is ultimately the view held at One First Street.

    [Note: The post above has been revised to clarify/correct my summary of the opinions. My initial phrasing was sloppy.].

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 17, 2026, 12:39 pm CST.

    Federal prosecutors urged jurors Monday to convict Chinese technology company Huawei, arguing that the company had grown by repeatedly committing crimes. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    Federal prosecutors urged jurors Monday to convict Chinese technology company Huawei, arguing during closing statements in the ongoing 11-week trial involving trade secrets theft and sanctions evasion that the company had grown by repeatedly committing crimes.

    According to a Monday story from Law.com, Meredith Arfa, the assistant U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Upcoming York, told jurors that Huawei spent two decades pursuing growth “by any means possible.”.

    To illustrate the trade secrets allegations, Arfa played a video of a former Huawei employee removing part of Tappy, T-Mobile’s robot for testing phone touchscreens, from the carrier’s lab. She also showed side-by-side images of Cisco’s and Huawei’s router source code, saying the two matched exactly—down to an engineer’s stray comment mentioning someone named “Bob.”.

    “This simply couldn’t happen without copying,” Arfa said in her summation.

    She further alleged that Huawei managers encouraged theft by paying bonuses for obtaining confidential competitor information, and that employees boasted about it on an internal forum.

    On the sanctions compliance allegations, prosecutors said Huawei secretly controlled Skycom, a subsidiary that supplied sensitive technology to Iran’s government. Arfa said the tech giant repeatedly lied about owning Skycom. She also pointed to admissions by Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer, who signed a deferred prosecution agreement after spending three years under house arrest. Meng acknowledged that Skycom’s operations violated U.S. sanctions, and that she misled HSBC, Huawei’s primary bank, about its compliance, Arfa noted.

    Huawei, one of the largest telecommunications companies in the world, denies the allegations, contending that the case rests on the independent actions of rogue employees who were disciplined.

    Recent findings suggest that the government confirmed the case in 2019. The company is represented by Jenner & Block, Sidley Austin and Steptoe.

    NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname.

    Industry observers note that in a federal complaint filed Tuesday in the Southern District of Newly introduced York, James stated he has been known as “Bron” since he was a young basketball standout in Ohio. He alleges that PlayVision and its co-founders, Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby, seek “to trade on” his “valuable name and reputation” by naming their app Bron.

    Industry observers note that there is no other connection between the word and the defendants or any other feature of their app, James alleges. He also argues in the complaint that when the defendants debuted a marketing campaign for the Bron app earlier this month, they used a video advertisement that incorporated an artificial intelligence-generated version of him.

    “The AI-generated version of Mr. James sits in an NBA-style locker room wearing a basketball jersey bearing Mr. James’s nickname, ‘Bron,’ above the number ‘23’—a number associated with Mr. James and the one he right now wears on the Philadelphia 76ers—with physical traits that mimic Mr. James, down to his identifiable tattoos,” according to the complaint.

    According to recent reports, “Speaking in Mr. James’s voice, the AI-generated Mr. James scrolls through wagers on other NBA players in defendants’ Bron app,” the complaint continues. “The ad then urges viewers to ‘scroll to bet.’”.

    The lawsuit seeks damages and an injunction preventing the defendants from using the “Bron” name; James’ name, image and likeness; and voice.

    Courthouse News Service has additional reporting.

    A representative for Bron did not respond to the publication’s request for comment.

Nye of the District of Idaho for attempting to provide material support and resources to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

Scott Proctor. “Alexander Scott Mercurio planned to attack that fundamental freedom by bringing death and destruction to several churches. This sentence demonstrates that the Department of Justice will relentlessly investigate, pursue, and prosecute those who would terrorize and murder Americans for exercising their religious rights.”.

    Sources indicate that “The sentencing of Mercurio today sends the clear message that where individuals intend to pursue acts of terrorism against the United States – whether in Coeur d’Alene, or any other community – they will be brought to justice,” said U.S. Attorney John C. Shirts for the District of Idaho. “Protecting our communities from terrorist activity is always the number one priority of this office and the Department of Justice.     In a recent development, “With today’s sentencing, this individual is being held accountable for pledging allegiance to ISIS and planning an attack on U.S. soil,” mentioned Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI works tirelessly to detect and prevent acts of terrorism in order to protect the American people. We will continue to work closely with our law enforcement and Justice Department partners to make sure anyone who participates in terrorist acts faces justice.”.

    The case was investigated by the FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force with assistance from the Coeur d’Alene Police Department, the Kootenai County Sheriff’s Office and the Ada County Sheriff’s Office.
